title: Food & drink
goal: Talk about food you like and don't like, say you're hungry or thirsty, and order in a restaurant or tea stall.
intro:
Food is at the heart of Marathi life — पोळी-भाजी at home, वडापाव and मिसळ on the street, and endless cups of चहा.

Grammatically, this unit introduces one of the most important patterns in Marathi: the **dative subject**. Instead of 'I like mangoes', Marathi says 'to me mangoes are pleasing' — **मला** आंबे आवडतात. The same pattern gives you 'I want', 'I need' and 'I'm hungry'.

vocab.note: n · verb: जेवणे 'to eat a meal'
f · Mumbai: चपाती. Sweet stuffed version: पुरणपोळी.
n · वरण-भात is classic Marathi comfort food. Spiced dal: आमटी.
m · 'cutting' (half-glass) चहा is a Mumbai institution.
m · pl आंबे. The Alphonso (हापूस) from Ratnagiri is Maharashtra's pride.
m · pl मासे. Coastal Konkan food is famous for fish.
Dative subject: मला आवडतं 'I like it'.
Agrees with the thing wanted: मला चहा हवा (m), पोळी हवी (f), पाणी हवं (n).
Invariable: मला पाणी पाहिजे. More common in Mumbai than हवं.
f · मला भूक लागली आहे 'I'm hungry'.
f · मला तहान लागली आहे 'I'm thirsty'.

phrases.en: Have you eaten? (to a man; a common caring greeting)

grammar.title: The dative subject: मला आवडतं, मला हवं
grammar.body:
With verbs of liking, wanting and needing, the person is put in the **dative** (-ला form) and the **thing** is the grammatical subject. The verb agrees with the thing.

Dative pronouns: **मला** (to me), **तुला** (to you, inf.), **त्याला** (to him), **तिला** (to her), **आम्हाला** (to us), **आपल्याला** (to us, incl.), **तुम्हाला** (to you, pol.), **त्यांना** (to them).

**आवडणे** 'to please': मला चहा आवडतो (m), मला कॉफी आवडते (f), मला दूध आवडतं (n), मला आंबे आवडतात (pl). Negative: आवडत नाही.

**हवा / हवी / हवं** 'wanted' agrees with the thing; **पाहिजे** 'needed' never changes. Both work for 'I want': मला चहा हवा / मला चहा पाहिजे.

grammar.title: Hunger, thirst and ordering
grammar.body:
Feelings that 'come over' you also use the dative, with the verb **लागणे** ('to strike, be felt'): मला भूक लागली 'hunger struck me' = I'm hungry. भूक and तहान are feminine, so the verb is लागली.

To order or ask for things, use the **polite imperative** (verb stem + -आ): द्या 'give', आणा 'bring', घ्या 'take / have', करा 'do'. Add ना or प्लीज to soften. Asking 'shall I…?' uses the stem + -ऊ: देऊ? 'shall I give?', आणू? 'shall I bring?'

examples.en: Could you bring a little salt?

dialogue.title: Misal in Pune
dialogue.setting: Rohan sits down at a busy misal-pav restaurant in Pune.

lines.speaker: Waiter
lines.en: Yes sir, what can I get you?

lines.speaker: Rohan
lines.native: एक मिसळ पाव आणि एक चहा.
lines.roman: ek misaḷ pāv āṇi ek tsahā.
lines.en: One misal pav and one tea.

lines.speaker: Waiter
lines.native: मिसळ तिखट हवी की कमी तिखट?
lines.roman: misaḷ tikhaṭ havī kī kamī tikhaṭ?
lines.en: Do you want the misal spicy or less spicy?

lines.speaker: Rohan
lines.native: मध्यम. मला खूप तिखट आवडत नाही.
lines.roman: madhyam. malā khūp tikhaṭ āvaḍat nāhī.
lines.en: Medium. I don't like it very spicy.

lines.speaker: Rohan
lines.en: Yes, bring a bottle of water.

culture: A traditional Marathi meal is served on a steel plate (ताट) with वरण-भात, पोळी, a भाजी, कोशिंबीर (salad), लोणचं (pickle) and perhaps a sweet. It's polite to take a second helping when offered — a host will insist ('अजून घ्या ना!'). **जेवलात का?** ('have you eaten?') is a common way of showing care. Street food classics: वडापाव (Mumbai's potato-fritter bun), मिसळ पाव (spicy sprouts curry, Pune/Nashik/Kolhapur styles), पोहे (flattened rice, the default breakfast) and साबुदाणा खिचडी on fasting days.
